Plastic surgery · published research

Pressure ulcer

Five mouse studies report selected improvements in wound repair or inflammatory markers, but use varying wavelengths and combinations. Animal findings do not resolve mixed clinical results.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Five mouse studies report selected improvements in wound repair or inflammatory markers, but use varying wavelengths and combinations. Animal findings do not resolve mixed clinical results.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact Pressure ulcer category contains 23 records; one additional mapped pressure-ulcer model appears under Mechanisms, for 24 relevant publications. The set includes 12 human randomized trials, two other human controlled studies, one case report, five mouse studies, three reviews, and one methodological paper. Records vary by ulcer stage, wavelength, and outcome measurement.

Human and clinical evidence

In 72 patients, a wavelength-comparison trial reported improved healing with 658-nm red light, while 808- and 940-nm arms did not show benefit (Taradaj et al. 2013). A sham-controlled trial in 86 people with stage III ulcers found no benefit from 904-nm treatment (Lucas et al. 2003). The 2025 RISE_UP randomized study included 48 participants, with 40 completing follow-up; blue-light treatment three times weekly for four weeks produced a greater mean PUSH-score reduction and more participants with a better trajectory, while the wound-area difference was not statistically significant because photographs were limited (Dollaku et al. 2025). A 38-person multispectral LED study found wound reduction in both active and sham groups without clear efficacy evidence (Lim et al. 2024). A 2018 follow-up biomarker study reported signals for 658 nm, but cohort independence from the earlier work is uncertain (Taradaj et al. 2018).

Animal evidence

Five mouse publications, including the mapped mechanistic record, examine wound repair or inflammatory markers. Several report selected favorable tissue outcomes, but models and protocols vary. These preclinical findings do not establish healing in human pressure ulcers.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro study was identified in the relevant records.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Clinical protocols span visible red, near-infrared, blue, and multispectral LEDs, delivered with different schedules and fluences. Ulcer stage, concurrent wound care, assessment scale, and follow-up differ. The contrast between positive 658-nm results and null near-infrared trials cautions against treating all wavelengths as equivalent. PUSH trajectory, ulcer area, and complete closure are distinct outcomes.

Interpretation

Trials reported better selected healing measures with some red- and blue-light protocols, alongside null results with other protocols. Differences in ulcer stage, dose, and measurement prevent a class-wide conclusion. Evidence does not establish a durable benefit across stages or devices.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for healing with selected red or blue-light protocols Very low for a class-wide effect across wavelengths and ulcer stages
Publications and records23 records; plus 1 mapped mechanistic pressure-ulcer model, 24 relevant publications.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Randomized pressure-ulcer trials show mixed, wavelength-specific results. Red 658-nm treatment and a 2025 blue-light trial reported selected healing measures, while 808/940-nm treatment and a 904-nm sham trial were null. A multispectral LED study did not establish clear superiority. Differences in stage, dose, and outcome measures limit pooling and generalization.
